questiontext.text: In an m-way search tree, how many keys and children may a node have at most?

answer.text: Up to m−1 keys and up to m children

feedback.text: Correct — m children are separated by m−1 ordered keys.

answer.text: Exactly 1 key and 2 children

feedback.text: That is the binary special case (m=2), not the general m-way node.

answer.text: Up to m keys and up to m−1 children

feedback.text: Reversed — children exceed keys by one.

answer.text: Unlimited keys and children

feedback.text: The order m caps both.

generalfeedback.text: An m-way search tree generalizes the BST: each node holds up to m−1 keys and points to up to m subtrees.

questiontext.text: An m-way search tree is best described as a generalization of which structure?

answer.text: The binary search tree, allowing more than two children per node

feedback.text: Correct — a BST is the m=2 case of an m-way search tree.

answer.text: The hash table

feedback.text: No — m-way trees are ordered comparison structures, not hashed.

answer.text: The heap

feedback.text: A heap orders by parent-child priority, not by ordered search keys.

answer.text: The linked list

feedback.text: A list has no branching search order.

generalfeedback.text: Raising the branching factor from 2 to m turns a binary search tree into an m-way search tree.

questiontext.text: How are keys and subtrees ordered within an m-way search tree node?

answer.text: Keys are sorted, and the subtree between two consecutive keys holds values in that range

feedback.text: Correct — the ordering generalizes the BST invariant to multiple keys.

answer.text: Keys are unordered; search must scan every subtree

feedback.text: No — ordered keys are what make it a search tree.

answer.text: All keys in a subtree exceed the root's largest key

feedback.text: Only the rightmost subtree does; each gap has its own range.

answer.text: Subtrees are ordered by size, not by key value

feedback.text: Ordering is by key value, enabling directed search.

generalfeedback.text: Ordered keys partition the key space; child i covers the interval between key i−1 and key i.

questiontext.text: What is the relationship between an m-way search tree and a B-tree?

answer.text: A B-tree is a balanced m-way search tree with minimum-occupancy constraints

feedback.text: Correct — the B-tree adds balancing and fill rules to the general m-way concept.

answer.text: They are completely unrelated structures

feedback.text: No — the B-tree is a special case of the m-way search tree.

answer.text: An m-way search tree is always balanced, a B-tree is not

feedback.text: Reversed — the B-tree adds the balance guarantee.

answer.text: A B-tree allows only two children, an m-way tree allows m

feedback.text: Both allow up to m children; the B-tree adds occupancy rules.

generalfeedback.text: The m-way search tree is the general concept; B-trees and B+ trees add the balancing rules that guarantee low height.

questiontext.text: A plain m-way search tree with no balancing rules can degenerate and give no height guarantee.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — without occupancy/balance rules it can become tall and unbalanced.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Only the added B-tree rules guarantee balance; the bare m-way tree does not.

questiontext.text: In an m-way search tree, a node holding k keys has exactly k+1 children.

answer.text: true

feedback.text: Correct — k ordered keys create k+1 key-space intervals, hence k+1 subtrees.

answer.text: false

feedback.text: Children always number one more than keys in a node.

questiontext.text: A ______ tree is the balanced special case of an m-way search tree, keeping all leaves at the same depth. (one letter/word, English)

answer.text: B

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: B-tree

feedback.text: Correct.

answer.text: B tree

feedback.text: Correct.

questiontext.text: Which statements about m-way search trees are true? (select all that apply)

answer.text: Each node has up to m children and up to m−1 ordered keys

feedback.text: Yes — this is the defining node shape.

answer.text: They are the general concept; B-trees and B+ trees add balancing rules

feedback.text: Yes — balanced variants build on the m-way idea.

answer.text: They always guarantee O(log n) height on their own

feedback.text: No — only balanced variants like the B-tree guarantee logarithmic height.

answer.text: They are limited to exactly two children per node

feedback.text: No — that is a binary search tree; an m-way node has up to m children.

generalfeedback.text: The m-way search tree generalizes the BST to m children with m−1 ordered keys; balance is not automatic and is what B-trees add.
